title: How to make tileset s, sprite charts and face charts.

posts.body:
Hello! I'm new on this of making games. I'm trying to make my games, but I've found a problem. I have many questions, to be honest!
(RPG Maker MV)

posts.author: Zia_
posts.body:
The technical part of your question is simple to answer. Your assets are arranged on sprite sheets, so (depending on asset type), several graphics fit into one grid that has specific guidelines to follow.
The maker knows where to "cut" those sprite sheets into single graphics.
I'd suggest to check the Help/Documentation about asset standards:
RPG Maker MV Help
Also, check out the RTP resources that come with the maker. You will quickly discover how they are arranged and what they have in common.
The artistic part ... depends on your artistic skills.
What I do in my game, as you want a more pixelated style (with a retro vibe, maybe?), I do all my assets in a 16x16px size and scale them up by 3 to 48x48px.
But I'd suggest to check what (free) assets are available to play around with them and learn to use the RPG Maker first. It might be a little early to think about doing all the assets from scratch right away.
By working with other peoples resources, they put out for you, you can get an idea and the experience, what works well and bad for you, and how these resources are created.

posts.author: Timeline_man
posts.body:
Here's a few answers, going in order asked.
1)
This tutorial
is very helpful for learning autotiles. It is a weird quirk of creating tiles in RPG Maker. As for tile sheets, that's a little more involved, but it's in the help file in the engine, with specifications about what goes where
2)Actor sprites are read as a portion of an image. The collision will always be 48 x 48 pixels, but you can make them any size. The sheet cells are divided into 8 segments, in 8 columns and 2 rows, and then each sprite in that cell is organized as a 3 x 4 grid, where each row is a direction, and each column is one part of a stepping animation. I'd look at the RTP sheets to get a better idea
3) I believe, without plugins, faces are 144 x 144 pixels, and a face sheet is made up of 8 faces, 2 rows, 8 columns.

posts.author: TeiRaven
posts.body:
Don't worry about putting it in the wrong section, it happens to everyone! A mod will move it to the right forum--in fact, Ms Littlefish is already on it as I type this.
Ninja'd. Several times. By several people. XD
First, you'll want to have a look at the resources that come with the engine, as well as the engine's Help file. The Help file has a section called "Asset Standards," and that tells you exactly how your resources should be structured in order to work correctly in the engine. Reading that, in conjunction with looking at the actual images the engine comes with, should help you get a clearer idea of how you'll need to format your own!
As far as "separating" the parts of different resources, I'm not entirely sure what you mean. Do you mean how big each tile of the tileset needs to be, and how big each frame of the sprite needs to be? That will all be covered in the Asset Standards, but MV operates on a 48px grid. Tilesets are made of a 16 x 16 grid of 48px squares. Sprites can be almost any size you'd like (just keep in mind how big they are compared to the world around them!), but they must be evenly divisible by 3 horizontally (because there are three frames across each one) and 4 vertically (because there are four directions down each one).
Making my sprites and tilesets is one of my favorite parts of making a game, and it's actually where I started in RPG Maker,
but!
I really, really recommend spending some time with the engine, getting a feel for how different pieces of it work, and modifying the default assets before you move on to making your own resources from scratch. It's much easier to start by, say, recoloring some walls and swapping in a new style of chair than it is to try doing an entire set from scratch! Just export a couple of sheets from the TIlesets section, make some changes on those copies, and import them under new names to get a feel for how the files behave when you import them.
For facesets specifically, I've had the most luck drawing them big and scaling them down--but I don't do very pixel-art-style faces. I'm not familiar with the ZENO (R) style you're referring to. Tiles and sprites, on the other hand, I always do at actual in-game size.

Resizing images is a basic function of every graphic editing program. Just make sure, to select a pixel-repeat mode, otherwise you will get blurry results. But don't worry about it too much right now. Just to keep in mind, this is what most games do, that look more "retro-ish".

As long as your main approach is to have fun, instead of matching any expectations, you'll have a great time. There are so many achievements ahead, as you get used to the RPG Maker more and more every day. Figure it out is fun, creating parts of your game as you wanted is fun, creating assets is fun, seeing them in your game for the first time moving around is fun ... Just don't overthink things. And if you get stuck, this community is always ready to help.
